title: The recovery method, and recovering commits I: a hard reset, a deleted branch, a deleted commit

slides.title: The recovery method, and recovering commits I: a hard reset, a deleted branch, a deleted commit

slides.caption: The plan was to drop the last commit, the last saved snapshot on the branch.
What the engineer does in the next sixty seconds decides the outcome.
The correct first step is one word.

slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
This is the guided pass. For each incident I read the symptom, ask the three questions, show the evidence command, then the anchor, then the repair.
The curriculum summary for this video describes the method in five words: stop, don't run maintenance, find the ID, anchor, repair.

slides.body: The three questions come from the first page of the chapter.
Then the method. Every recovery follows the same eight steps.

slides.direction: The eight steps of section 13.7, one at a time.
items: Stop. Do not run another command that moves refs or deletes files, and do not run git gc, git prune, git clean or git stash clear. Waiting loses nothing; a second "fix" can.

Record the symptom and the last commands. Copy the terminal scrollback if you have it. Git prints the ID you need in more places than people remember: Deleted branch x (was 2f65488), Dropped refs/stash@{0} (...), HEAD is now at ..., the warning on leaving detached HEAD.
Classify. Was the work committed, stashed, staged, or only saved? That decides the layer (section 13.2) and whether to continue with Git at all.
Find the ID. From the scrollback, the branch reflog, the HEAD reflog, ORIG_HEAD, git fsck, or another repository, in that order.

slides.direction: The eight steps of section 13.7, one at a time.
items: Anchor it. git branch rescue/<what> <id>. An anchored commit cannot expire.
Inspect before you move anything. git log, git show --stat, git diff, git range-diff, git cherry against the anchor.
Integrate with the lowest-risk move. Prefer adding (a branch, a cherry-pick, a merge) over rewinding, and git reset --keep over git reset --hard (Chapter 11, section 11.6).
Verify, then clean up. Prove that the result holds what was lost, and only then delete the rescue branch.

slides.direction: The decision flow of section 13.7: where to look. Reveal it branch by branch, and for each branch name the layer.
slides.text:
Was the lost work ever committed, stashed, or staged with "git add"?
   |
   +-- no ----> Git has no object. Editor history, IDE local history, backups, Time Machine.   (13.12)
   |
   +-- staged only ----> git fsck --lost-found ; look in .git/lost-found/other                  (13.9)
   |
   +-- stashed, then dropped or cleared ----> git fsck --unreachable | ... git log --merges     (13.9)
   |
   +-- committed
        |
        +-- Do you have the ID (scrollback, CI log, pull request, chat)? -- yes --> git branch rescue <id>
        |
        +-- Did a branch move (reset, rebase, merge, amend, cherry-pick)?
        |      --> git reflog show <branch> ; take the entry below the bad operation            (13.8)
        |
        +-- Is the branch itself gone, or was the work done in detached HEAD?
        |      --> git reflog (HEAD) ; or git fsck --no-reflogs for the dangling tips           (13.8)
        |
        +-- Did the server lose it (force push, deleted remote branch)?
        |      --> git reflog show origin/<branch> ; a teammate's clone ; the host's tools      (13.10, 13.15)
        |
        +-- No reflog entry anywhere (pruned fetch, expired log, other machine)?
               --> git fsck --lost-found ; then another clone, a bundle, a backup               (13.6, 13.14)

slides.body: The usual complication, said now so that you recognise it in the lab: if you committed new work on the shortened branch before you noticed, a reset back to the old tip trades one loss for another.
The same slip without --hard is milder.

items: Running a clean-up command during the incident. Root cause: git gc, git prune, git stash clear and git reflog expire remove the names and objects that the recovery depends on.
Deleting the repository and cloning again. Root cause: reflogs are local and start with the clone, and the clone has none of the unpushed objects.
Using HEAD@{1} some commands later. Root cause: any later movement, even a switch, shifts the positions; search with --grep-reflog and use the full ID.
Repairing before anchoring. Root cause: a found commit is still unreachable from refs; until a branch names it, a failed repair or an expiry can lose it again.
Resetting a branch back to recover one commit. Root cause: the reset discards commits made since; copy the missing commit forward instead.

beats.text: The plan was to drop the last commit, the last saved snapshot on the branch. A hard reset moves the branch back and overwrites your files. The typo was a 3 where a 1 was meant. Three commits and their changes are gone from the branch and from the working tree.

beats.text: What the engineer does in the next sixty seconds decides the outcome. One option is to search the web, find a command that "cleans up the repository", and run it. Another is to delete the directory and clone again. Both destroy the thing that would have saved the work: the first removes the evidence, and the second produces a clone with no reflog, Git's local log of where each name has pointed, and none of the unpushed objects. The textbook calls re-cloning "the classic non-fix".

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. In the last two videos you learned what Git keeps and for how long. Today that knowledge becomes a procedure of eight steps, and you apply it three times: to a hard reset, to a deleted branch, and to a commit that vanished from the middle of a branch.

Today that knowledge becomes a procedure of eight steps, and you apply it three times: to a hard reset, to a deleted branch, and to a commit that vanished from the middle of a branch.

beats.text: This is the guided pass. For each incident I read the symptom, ask the three questions, show the evidence command, then the anchor, then the repair. In the labs you repeat all three from the symptoms alone.

beats.text: The curriculum summary for this video describes the method in five words: stop, don't run maintenance, find the ID, anchor, repair. The textbook's section 13.7 has eight numbered steps, and that is the version you get here.

beats.text: The three questions come from the first page of the chapter. Was the work ever written into the object database? Does anything still name it? Has the clock run out? The first answer decides whether Git can help at all. The second tells you the layer. The third tells you the deadline.
beats.tele: The three questions come from the first page of the chapter. Was the work ever written into the object database? Does anything still name it? Has the clock run out? The first answer decides whether Git can help at all. The second tells you the layer. The third tells you the deadline.

beats.text: Then the method. Every recovery follows the same eight steps.
beats.tele: Then the method. Every recovery follows the same eight steps.

beats.text: One. Stop. Don't run another command that moves refs or deletes files, and don't run git gc, git prune, git clean or git stash clear. Waiting loses nothing. A second "fix" can.
beats.tele: One. Stop. Don't run another command that moves refs or deletes files, and don't run `git gc`, `git prune`, `git clean` or `git stash clear`. Waiting loses nothing. A second "fix" can.

beats.text: Two. Record the symptom and the last commands. Copy the terminal scrollback if you have it. Git prints the ID you need in more places than people remember: "Deleted branch x (was ...)", "Dropped refs/stash@{0}", "HEAD is now at", the warning on leaving detached HEAD, when you are on no branch.
beats.tele: Two. Record the symptom and the last commands. Copy the terminal scrollback if you have it. Git prints the ID you need in more places than people remember: "Deleted branch x (was ...)", "Dropped refs/stash@{0}", "HEAD is now at", the warning on leaving detached HEAD, when you are on no branch.

beats.text: Three. Classify. Was the work committed, stashed, staged, or only saved? That decides the layer, and whether to continue with Git at all.
beats.tele: Three. Classify. Was the work committed, stashed, staged, or only saved? That decides the layer, and whether to continue with Git at all.

beats.text: Four. Find the ID. From the scrollback, the branch reflog, the HEAD reflog, ORIG_HEAD, git fsck, or another repository, in that order.
beats.tele: Four. Find the ID. From the scrollback, the branch reflog, the HEAD reflog, `ORIG_HEAD`, `git fsck`, or another repository, in that order.

beats.text: Five. Anchor it. git branch rescue/<what> <id>. A branch is a name for a commit, and an anchored commit can't expire.
beats.tele: Five. Anchor it. `git branch rescue/<what> <id>`. A branch is a name for a commit, and an anchored commit can't expire.

beats.text: Six. Inspect before you move anything. git log, git show --stat, git diff, git range-diff, git cherry against the anchor.
beats.tele: Six. Inspect before you move anything. `git log`, `git show --stat`, `git diff`, `git range-diff`, `git cherry` against the anchor.

beats.text: Seven. Integrate with the lowest-risk move. Prefer adding, a branch, a cherry-pick or a merge, over rewinding. And prefer git reset --keep over git reset --hard.
beats.tele: Seven. Integrate with the lowest-risk move. Prefer adding, a branch, a cherry-pick or a merge, over rewinding. And prefer `git reset --keep` over `git reset --hard`.

beats.text: Eight. Verify, then clean up. Prove that the result holds what was lost, and only then delete the rescue branch.
beats.tele: Eight. Verify, then clean up. Prove that the result holds what was lost, and only then delete the rescue branch.

beats.text: Why is the anchor a separate step, before any repair? Because of what it costs and what it buys. 🟢 SAFE: git branch rescue/x <id> leaves the working tree, the index, HEAD and the current branch unchanged. It adds one ref with a new reflog. In exchange, the commit moves from layer two or three to layer one, and no expiry or collection can touch it. After that, every repair you attempt is reversible.
beats.tele: Why is the anchor a separate step, before any repair? Because of what it costs and what it buys. 🟢 SAFE: `git branch rescue/x <id>` leaves the working tree, the index, HEAD and the current branch unchanged. It adds one ref with a new reflog. In exchange, the commit moves from layer two or three to layer one, and no expiry or collection can touch it. After that, every repair you attempt is reversible.

beats.text: When not to follow the method to its end, from section 13.17. Don't recover a secret: if the "lost" commit contains a credential, restoring it puts the credential back on a branch, so rotate first. Don't rewind shared history to recover: on a branch that others have pulled, add commits. And recovered isn't verified: a branch that points at the right commit proves nothing about the working tree you now have. Run the tests.
beats.tele: When not to follow the method to its end, from section 13.17. Don't recover a secret: if the "lost" commit contains a credential, restoring it puts the credential back on a branch, so rotate first. Don't rewind shared history to recover: on a branch that others have pulled, add commits. And recovered isn't verified: a branch that points at the right commit proves nothing about the working tree you now have. Run the tests.

beats.text: Think of a recovery as moving a box in the vault back under an index card. In all the accidents of today, the box never left the vault. The commit never stopped existing. What was lost was the card: the ref that named it.
beats.tele: Think of a recovery as moving a box in the vault back under an index card. In all the accidents of today, the box never left the vault. The commit never stopped existing. What was lost was the card: the ref that named it.

beats.text: So every one of these recoveries ends with the same act: a ref is pointed at a commit that never stopped existing. The hard part isn't the repair. It's finding the right box number, and not ordering a clear-out while you search.
beats.tele: So every one of these recoveries ends with the same act: a ref is pointed at a commit that never stopped existing. The hard part isn't the repair. It's finding the right box number, and not ordering a clear-out while you search.

beats.text: Where this picture breaks: it covers committed work only. Uncommitted work that a hard reset overwrote was never in a box, or was a single blob without a card. That's a different video.
beats.tele: Where this picture breaks: it covers committed work only. Uncommitted work that a hard reset overwrote was never in a box, or was a single blob without a card. That's a different video.

beats.tele: Today's three incidents are three branches of the "committed" subtree. Try it now, thirty seconds: point at the branch of this tree for each of the three. Then say your answer.

beats.text: The hard reset: a branch moved. The deleted branch: the branch itself is gone. The dropped commit: a branch moved, through a rebase.
beats.tele: The hard reset: a branch moved. The deleted branch: the branch itself is gone. The dropped commit: a branch moved, through a rebase.

beats.text: "HEAD is now at 798cb66". Three commits shorter.
beats.tele: "HEAD is now at 798cb66". Three commits shorter.

beats.text: Stop, and ask the three questions. Was the work an object? Yes, three commits. On the picture they turn dashed, and they still exist. Does anything name it? Predict which three places. Say it out loud. I'll wait.
beats.tele: Stop, and ask the three questions. Was the work an object? Yes, three commits. On the picture they turn dashed, and they still exist. Does anything name it? Predict which three places. Say it out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: The HEAD reflog, ORIG_HEAD and the branch reflog, and they agree: the old tip is 495f3a9.
beats.tele: The HEAD reflog, `ORIG_HEAD` and the branch reflog, and they agree: the old tip is `495f3a9`.

beats.text: ORIG_HEAD is safe to use here, because git reset wrote it and nothing has run since. Anchor, look, move.
beats.tele: `ORIG_HEAD` is safe to use here, because `git reset` wrote it and nothing has run since. Anchor, look, move.

beats.text: The rescue branch lists all six commits. The branch is back at 495f3a9. ORIG_HEAD moves as well, because this reset wrote it again. The lost commits were on layer two, the reflogs, for the whole time. Those are the three commits from the opening.

beats.text: The usual complication, said now so that you recognise it in the lab: if you committed new work on the shortened branch before you noticed, a reset back to the old tip trades one loss for another. Anchor both tips, reset to the one you want as the base, and cherry-pick the commits from the other.

beats.text: A mixed reset moves the branch and the index and leaves the working tree alone. The content of the two "missing" commits is still in your files, shown as modifications. A second mixed reset to HEAD@{1} puts the branch and the index back, and the status is clean.

It is 🔴 DANGEROUS, because it deletes the ref together with its reflog. It also prints the one fact you need: "(was 2f65488)". Step two of the method: copy the scrollback.

beats.text: The commits are on layer three now. Quick quiz, two options. Does plain git fsck, without --no-reflogs, find them: yes, or no? Say it out loud.

A week later a colleague needs two of its commits for a new training run. He had fetched the branch and never checked it out, and his nightly fetch runs with pruning.

beats.text: He classifies first: committed work, no ref, no reflog entry in his clone, so layer three, with a deadline. He doesn't run anything that might trigger a collection. git fsck --lost-found gives one dangling commit. A log of that tip with --not --all shows exactly the two commits and their author.

beats.text: He anchors the tip, pushes the branch so that a second repository holds it, and only then tells the author that the experiment is back under a new branch name. The incident note gives the full commit ID, not a selector.

And it ends with what you'll say to the person who asked, in terms of confidence and deadline, not in terms of commands.
